system:
You are the Network operator and regulator reviewer, standing in for the telecom regulator and mobile operators (cell broadcast delivery). You check that the message can be delivered and read on a handset: required languages present, no language over the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, the encoding, and that the first page carries the hazard and the action.
You see only each language's phone text with its character count, encoding and page count, and the profile's required languages. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

data.summary: Delivery checks pass: Arabic and English are both present, Arabic is UCS-2 and English is GSM-7, and both are under the 15-page maximum (8 and 3 pages). Two problems remain. First, neither language's first page gives an action for the fog hazard. Second, both texts end with an unrelated, unverified report of a dam burst near Al Ain plus an order to leave the area. That evacuation order is the only action in the message, and it sits on the last page. A person must decide whether the dam report is real and, if so, whether it needs its own alert.

objections.issue: Neither language puts an action on the first page. The English first page (about 93 GSM-7 characters) and the Arabic first page (41 UCS-2 characters) carry only the fog hazard. The message gives no protective action for fog. The only action ('leave the area now') is at the very end, on page 3 in English and page 8 in Arabic, and it belongs to a different hazard.
objections.fix: Add a short fog action right after the hazard in both languages, so it lands on page 1 (e.g. 'Avoid travel; if driving, slow down and use low beams'). Keep the Arabic action within the first 41 characters where possible.

evidence.quote: Fog warning: thick fog may cut visibility to zero at times across western regions of the UAE
An emergency alert message shall be immediately recognizable

objections.issue: Both language versions end with an unrelated, unattributed report of a dam burst near Al Ain and an evacuation order. Only the National Center for Meteorology is cited as source, and that is for the fog. Handsets will show this evacuation order with emergency status, so people could act on an unverified claim. If the dam report is true, it is buried on the last page of a fog warning.
objections.fix: A person must decide. If the dam report cannot be verified, remove the sentence from both languages. If it is verified, issue it as a separate alert for the affected area, with the hazard and action on page 1 and a named source.
